data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A coin system C is canonical if and only if the greedy algorithm is optimal for all amounts w in the bounded range [c_2 + 1, c_1 + c_2 - 1]. The smallest counterexample can be found by checking this finite range using dynamic programming versus the greedy approach, yielding a pseudo-polynomial algorithm O(n * (c_1 + c_2)). A truly polynomial-time algorithm in n alone is achievable (e.g., Pearson's O(n^3) algorithm), but this candidate does not implement it.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The bound c_1 + c_2 - 1 is asserted from memory without a sandboxed Python simulation as required by the problem contract; a single enumerated coin system whose smallest counterexample exceeds this bound would refute it outright.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"The range [c_2 + 1, c_1 + c_2 - 1] may be incorrect or have an off-by-one error, which would cause false positives or negatives.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"The claim that a polynomial-time algorithm in n alone exists is unproven here and relies on unverified external knowledge.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"By the theorem attributed to Kozen and Zaks (1994), if a counterexample exists for a coin system, the smallest counterexample amount must be strictly less than c_1 + c_2. Thus, it suffices to test each amount w from c_2 + 1 up to c_1 + c_2 - 1. For each w, compute the greedy representation and compare its coin count to the optimal count found via dynamic programming. If any w yields a greedy count greater than the optimal count, return w as the smallest counterexample. If no such w exists in this range, C is canonical. This procedure terminates because the range is finite, and its worst-case time complexity is O(n * (c_1 + c_2)), which is pseudo-polynomial as it depends on the magnitude of the largest coin.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
